How does the internet know where to go?You only typed a name. How does the internet know which machine to send you to?

PromiseThe internet doesn't know names: DNS turns a site's name into a number (its IP address), then your request goes out as packets labelled with that number, passed router to router to the server, and the page comes back to your address the same way.
AudienceCurious teens and adults anywhere who use the internet every day but have never seen what happens after they press Enter. They may have heard of 'IP addresses' or 'DNS', but not how the pieces fit together.
Length60.86 s · 20 shots · 52 drawn frames · 1920×1080 · 60 fps · en · voice: Catherine
LookIsometric template (Isometric diorama) · #ff5d8f #7b8cff
The Isometric template: one small diorama at a time floating on soft pastel #eef1ff, always at the same 30-degree isometric angle, lit from the upper left (each face of a block a step lighter or darker) with a soft periwinkle shadow under each slab. Clean matte blocks with rounded edges in periwinkle, peach, mint and butter, ink #2d3047 for type. The one saturated accent, #ff5d8f (as in the template's golden stills), is only ever your request: its packets and the number it needs. Tiny faceless figures. Captions: every spoken line as a subtitle (subtitles on) in the template's soft white pill, a few words at a time, the starred key word in #ff5d8f (film.css sets .caption .key to the accent, as the template's proof did; the look's own key colour is periwinkle). No grain, no bloom; very soft ambient occlusion.
The storyboard passes the standard: 20 shots, 52 drawn frames, 13 facts, 6 acts.

Fact sheet

IdClaimSource
f1DNS turns the name you type into an IP address, the number that identifies the server, so the browser can contact it. The lookup is done by a DNS resolver; your Wi-Fi router is usually set to use your ISP's resolver.Cloudflare Learning Paths, 'What is DNS?' (developers.cloudflare.com/learning-paths/cybersafe/concepts/what-is-dns/, updated 23 Apr 2026): 'DNS translates the domain name that you type in the browser ... to a computer-friendly IP address'; 'Your Wi-Fi router is typically preconfigured to send DNS queries to the resolver owned by your ISP.' RFC 1034 (Mockapetris, 1987), Domain Concepts and Facilities.
f2The network moves packets by number, not by name: every IP packet's header carries a 32-bit source address and a 32-bit destination address, and a router looks up the destination address in its routing table to choose where to send it next. Names exist only in DNS. The router panel is a simplified routing table: its 'route A/B/C' stand for the router's outgoing links, and each row starts with a real address prefix used in the film (Wikimedia Asia 103.102.166.0/24, a.root-servers.net 198.41.0.4, ns0.wikimedia.org 208.80.154.238).RFC 791, Internet Protocol, §3.1 ('Source Address: 32 bits', 'Destination Address: 32 bits'); RFC 1812, Requirements for IPv4 Routers, §5.2.4.3 ('the router looks up the IP Destination Address in its routing table to determine an appropriate next hop address').
f3An IPv4 address is 32 bits, four octets; written as four decimal numbers, each part is one octet, 8 bits, so 2^8 = 256 values: 0 to 255. Simplification: the film shows IPv4 only; id.wikipedia.org also has an IPv6 address (2001:df2:e500:ed1a::1, 128 bits).RFC 791 §2.3: 'Addresses are fixed length of four octets (32 bits).' RFC 8200 (IPv6, 128-bit addresses). The IPv6 address checked as f4.
f4The film's real example, and where it was looked up: from Australian networks (Telstra and Optus address blocks), en.wikipedia.org (a CNAME of dyna.wikimedia.org) resolves to 103.102.166.224. That address's reverse name is text-lb.eqsin.wikimedia.org: Wikimedia's caching data centre 'eqsin' at Equinix SG3, Singapore (listed by Wikitech as in service since 2017), and Wikimedia's GeoDNS map sends Australia (AU) to eqsin first. The block 103.102.166.0/24 is registered to Wikimedia at APNIC (WIKIMEDIA-AP). So for a viewer in Australia the page really comes from Singapore; the film says 'you, in Australia' on screen and 'from Australia' in the script. Elsewhere the answer differs (from the UK, for instance, the same name gave 185.15.59.224, Wikimedia's Amsterdam site).Checked 2026-11-23 with Google Public DNS (dns.google/resolve, type A, edns_client_subnet 1.120.0.0/13 and 101.160.0.0/11 (Telstra) and 49.176.0.0/12 (Optus), owners checked with APNIC RDAP; all three answered 103.102.166.224; PTR text-lb.eqsin.wikimedia.org); Wikimedia operations-dns 'geo-maps' (raw.githubusercontent.com/wikimedia/operations-dns/master/geo-maps), line 'AU => [eqsin, ulsfo, ...] # Australia'; Wikitech 'Data centers' and 'Eqsin data center' (wikitech.wikimedia.org); APNIC RDAP for 103.102.166.224 (WIKIMEDIA-AP). UK check: subnets 86.128.0.0/10 (BT), 2.96.0.0/13, 62.30.0.0/15 → 185.15.59.224, PTR text-lb.esams.wikimedia.org.
f5The analogy: DNS is like a phone book (here, your phone's contacts): you look up a name, and what is used to reach someone is the number. The contact's number on screen is masked ('04•• ••• •••', the shape of an Australian mobile number); it stands for no real number.Cloudflare Learning Paths, 'What is DNS?' (as f1): 'The Domain Name System (DNS) is the phonebook of the Internet ... similar to how a phonebook translates a person's name to a phone number.'
f6When it has nothing cached, the resolver walks the chain: a root name server refers it to the servers for the top-level domain (.org), those refer it to the domain's own name servers (wikipedia.org: ns0, ns1, ns2.wikimedia.org), and those hold the address. Real names on screen: the .org servers are run by Public Interest Registry (v0n0.pir-ns.org, 199.19.56.1); ns0.wikimedia.org is 208.80.154.238. Simplifications: the CNAME step (en.wikipedia.org → dyna.wikimedia.org, answered by the same Wikimedia name servers) is folded into one answer; a busy resolver usually already has the root's and .org's referrals cached, so most lookups skip the first steps.Cloudflare Learning Paths, 'What is DNS?' (the lookup diagram: resolver → root nameserver → .com nameserver → example.com nameserver → IP); RFC 1034 §5.3.3 (the resolver's algorithm); NS and A records checked 2026-11-23 with Google Public DNS (org NS: v0n0...v2n1.pir-ns.org; wikipedia.org NS: ns0/ns1/ns2.wikimedia.org).
f7The root of DNS is served by 13 named root servers (a to m.root-servers.net) run by 12 independent organisations, as 2,046 operational instances around the world, in many countries (Australia and Singapore included). On screen: '13 names · 2,046 servers'. a.root-servers.net is 198.41.0.4 (Verisign).Root Server Technical Operations Association, root-servers.org (read 2026-11-23T15:48Z: 'the root server system consists of 2046 operational instances operated by the 12 independent root server operators'); IANA, 'Root Servers' (iana.org/domains/root/servers): 13 named authorities and their addresses.
f8A resolver keeps (caches) each answer for its TTL, a time in seconds set by the domain's owner. Wikimedia's zone gives dyna.wikimedia.org a TTL of 180 seconds (3 minutes); the CNAME from en.wikipedia.org has a much longer TTL (Google Public DNS still had 20,026 s, about five and a half hours, left on it). On screen: '180 seconds'; the script says 'a few minutes'.RFC 1034 §3.6: 'TTL ... is primarily used by resolvers when they cache RRs. The TTL describes how long a RR can be cached before it should be discarded.' Wikimedia operations-dns, templates/wikimedia.org: 'dyna 180 IN DYNA geoip!text-addrs'; Google Public DNS answers on 2026-11-23 showed TTL 180 for the A record.
f9Your request travels as packets (IP datagrams). TCP carries the data as segments, each sent as one IP datagram, numbered so the far end can put them back in order and ask again for any that are lost. Simplifications: the film shows the page request as one packet and leaves out the TCP and TLS handshakes that come first, and the encryption (HTTPS).RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol, §2.2: 'The application byte-stream is conveyed over the network via TCP segments, with each TCP segment sent as an Internet Protocol (IP) datagram'; reliability 'via sequence numbers ... correction via retransmission'. RFC 791 §3.1 for the header's addresses.
f10Routing on the internet is hop by hop: no router holds the whole route; each one only decides the next hop for the packet's destination address, from its own table, and passes the packet on.RFC 1812 §5.2.4.3 (next hop chosen from the destination address) and §7.3.2 ('the hop-by-hop routing paradigm generally used throughout the current Internet').
f11Traffic between countries goes almost entirely over submarine fibre cables; satellites carry a very small share (the FCC counts 0.37% of U.S. international capacity). Australia has no land link to anywhere, so packets to Singapore cross the sea in a cable. Example on screen: INDIGO-West, Perth – Jakarta – Singapore (Tuas), 4,600 km, in service since 2019, Telstra among its owners. Which cable a given packet uses depends on the ISP's routes; the film labels it 'example'.TeleGeography, 'Submarine Cable FAQs' (www2.telegeography.com/submarine-cable-faqs-frequently-asked-questions); TeleGeography Submarine Cable Map, 'INDIGO-West' (submarinecablemap.com/api/v3/cable/indigo-west.json: length 4,600 km; landing points Perth, Jakarta, Tuas; RFS May 2019; owners AARNet, Google, Indosat Ooredoo, Singtel, Superloop, Telstra).
f12The reply comes in many packets. English Wikipedia's Main Page HTML alone was 52,254 bytes compressed (gzip) on 2026-11-23 (a second fetch gave 52,307: the page changes). A packet on a normal 1,500-byte (Ethernet) link carries at most 1,500 − 20 (IPv4 header) − 20 (TCP header) = 1,460 bytes of data, so 52,254 / 1,460 = 35.79 → about 36 packets, before the images and styles, which come in more. On screen: 'page text alone ≈ 36 packets'. Simplifications: TLS and HTTP/2 framing overheads are ignored, which would add a few.Measured with curl on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page with Accept-Encoding: gzip (size_download 52,254 and 52,307 bytes), 2026-11-23; RFC 894 (IP over Ethernet, 1,500-byte maximum); RFC 791 (20-byte minimum IPv4 header); RFC 9293 (20-byte minimum TCP header). The arithmetic is in storyboard.build.py.
f13The reply is addressed to the source address the request carried, so it comes back to you. Simplification: most homes and mobile networks share one public IPv4 address through NAT; the reply reaches that shared address, and the router (or the operator's NAT) hands it on to your phone. The film says 'addressed to you'.RFC 791 §3.1 (source address in every datagram); RFC 3022, Traditional IP Network Address Translator.

Music

Composed for this film (ElevenLabs Music, music/bed.mp3) · 100 BPM · A light electronic bed, as the template's Sound line asks: soft marimba-like plucks and a warm round sub, a glassy pad, a brushed shaker, no lead melody, composed to the take's length. It thins under the DNS chain (s07 to s11) so the blips read, lifts as the packet crosses the sea (s15) and resolves on the recap; it runs on past the last frame into the opening for the loop. Effects, small and clean: a soft click or pop for every block that rises, a tick for each tag, a blip at each server or router a cube reaches, a paper flick for each answer card, a drawer click and clock tick for the cache, a bubbly whoosh under the sea, a ripple of pops as the reply's packets leave the server, a chime when the page completes. The cuts follow the take.
